issue_context.title: Add CollectionsMarshal.SetCount API for List<T>
comments: IMO this would be more useful and discoverable as an instance method `List<T>.Resize(int newCount)`, which also zero-inits the buffer if needed. Zero-initing is surprisingly cheap; and it can be elided entirely if _T_ contains gcrefs, as you called out; and it can also be elided if the underlying array ends up being resized as a result of the operation.

While an instance Resize that'd zero-init would be more discoverable, I'd rather add both APIs than just it, since probably a lot of the usecases for AsSpan that'd modify don't care about the contents of it, so it'd only prove to be an unnecessary cost.
Would adding both an instance Resize with zero init and not as exposed SetCount without it be an acceptable solution?

Edit: I guess there could also be an optional parameter, something like `bool initElements = true`

Could I get some movement on the proposal @eiriktsarpalis? It's been sitting as `api-needs-work` for the past few months, with the only change being it getting added to the work planned for .Net 7, but I'm afraid it won't get there due to not being approved yet.

> It's been sitting as api-needs-work for the past few months, with the only change being it getting added to the work planned for .Net 7, but I'm afraid it won't get there due to not being approved yet.

As a meta point aside, it takes work to review API proposals, validate that the concept is something we want included, ensure the design makes sense given the rest of what's exposed, etc.  That work all happens prior to an issue being marked as API approved.  So the fact that it was added to the cited "planned work" issue is in fact movement.

@MichalPetryka I'm also not in favor of this API as proposed, I much more like @GrabYourPitchforks's proposal. If you care about perf why do you use List rather than pre-allocated buffer. Perhaps I also simply cannot see end to end scenario where I'd use List with RNG.Fill and care much about perf. Perhaps if you shared E2E scenario it would be more convincing

RNG was used as an example API that takes in a span, if you want a more real usecase the example span AddRange from https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/1530#issuecomment-966455158 shows a scenario with less overhead. I'd be fine with a general purpose API as proposed by @GrabYourPitchforks, but an "unsafe" version would still be useful, even for example in that proposed AddRange to avoid the overhead of writing the data there twice.

I'll suggest to change proposal to what @GrabYourPitchforks has suggested and once you have that API perhaps create a second proposal (only if you feel you'll need it - perhaps share a benchmark with potential perf improvement to support that)

I've tried benchmarking both a zeroing and a non zeroing version with an AddRange from #1530 adding 50 ints each to an empty list with preallocated memory, but me and 3 other people have gotten wildly different results:
Me:
```
|     Method |     Mean |    Error |   StdDev |
|----------- |---------:|---------:|---------:|
|    Zeroing | 70.31 ns | 0.411 ns | 0.365 ns |
| NonZeroing | 11.34 ns | 0.269 ns | 0.224 ns |
```
One person:
```
|     Method |     Mean |    Error |   StdDev |
|----------- |---------:|---------:|---------:|
|    Zeroing | 21.79 ns | 0.500 ns | 0.545 ns |
| NonZeroing | 14.88 ns | 0.295 ns | 0.340 ns |
```
Another person:
```
|     Method |     Mean |    Error |   StdDev |
|----------- |---------:|---------:|---------:|
|    Zeroing | 28.67 ns | 0.207 ns | 0.194 ns |
| NonZeroing | 10.20 ns | 0.012 ns | 0.011 ns |
```
@tannergooding:
```
|     Method |      Mean |     Error |    StdDev |
|----------- |----------:|----------:|----------:|
|    Zeroing | 11.600 ns | 0.1619 ns | 0.1514 ns |
| NonZeroing |  6.739 ns | 0.0170 ns | 0.0159 ns |
```
While the ratios are completely different, they all show a clear win for a non zeroing version, so I'd prefer both to be exposed. (I have absolutely no idea what would cause the ratio to be so wildly different on my machine, but it persists on every single run)

As a workaround I've used a
```
EmptyCollection<T>(int count) : ICollection<T>
    Count => count
    CopyTo(...) => {}

new List(emptyCollection)
```

After this CollectionMarshal will return a full-range span.

This allows to skip zero initialization and EmptyCollection instance can be cached. But it's a quirk based on current list behaviour (I doubt it will change tho).
@layomia, I see you assigned this to yourself.  Does that mean you're working on this?
@stephentoub yes.

I personally am not a big fan of the decision to not zero the non-gc elements, somebody someday will shoot their leg with this:
```csharp
List<int> a = Enumerable.Range(0, 1024).ToList();

a.SetCount(10);  // doesn't clear upper 1024-10 elements. OK
    ...
a.SetCount(100); // doesn't clear on expansion either. Not OK
                 // I now have garbage in my upper 90 elements
```
(as in implemented in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/80311)
cc @GrabYourPitchforks

This is a lowlevel API where the intent of use is for developers to write their own performant APIs that extend `List<T>`s functionality.

It exists in the `CollectionsMarshal` class under the `System.Runtime.InteropServices` namespace, both of which API review have agreed indicate the "unsafeness" of the APIs exposed.

The API can be used "incorrectly" but the intended usage scenario is that after `a.SetCount(100);` the developer explicitly initialize the `n` (`90` in this case) "newly visible" elements. Thus, for the intended use-case, zeroing is doing needless throwaway work since the API author will be immediately overwriting the elements themselves.

It is no more unsafe than `module:SkipLocalsInit` or `Unsafe.SkipInit` and is certainly more visibly unsafe than the former.

Particularly for large `T` and for large mutations, the zeroing and additional cache updates can quickly add up and negatively impact the performance of the application. Requiring zeroing for all types would hurt the main usage scenario of the API and ultimately result in people coming and asking for yet another API that does allow skipping the zeroing with the API that does zero then being under utilized.

`module:SkipLocalsInit`, `Unsafe.SkipInit`, `GC.AllocateUninitialized` all **explicitly** state that you'll have to deal with possibly junk data. This API doesn't. Anyway, just wanted to highlight my concern.

> under the System.Runtime.InteropServices namespace, both of which API review have agreed indicate the "unsafeness"

Honestly, it doesn't read for me as "it's unsafe", but rather "a set of tools to help with interop"

Interop and marshalling is by definition unsafe.

It's one of the many things we'd mark as `UnsafeCallersOnly` if such a concept existed.

That's why we didn't name this `SetCountUnsafe` for example, because we believe that it being in `CollectionsMarshal` implies that.

review_comments: Why is this needed?
Oh, size not Capacity, nevermind.
Is there a use case for setting a value smaller than the current count? That's already possible with RemoveRange.
Having the API not support it would certainly be unexpected.

Would it? Trying to set Capacity to less than Count throws. How is this different? And what's the use case where you'd call this to shrink rather than grow? I'm not against it if it's useful, I'm trying to understand the use.
It'd be useful in cases where you don't know whether the count will be smaller or bigger than the list size.
What's an example of that?
Updating data in an existing list with an API that can return less data.
I don't follow. Isn't that Clear then AddRange? Can you share a concrete example with code so I can understand a real case where this would be valuable?

Ultimately we have a check here that's either: `if (count < list._size) { throw }` or we have `if (count < list._size) { ClearIfReferenceOrContainsReferences(); list._size = count }`.

Not throwing is less confusing and makes the API more flexible. It's already unsafe and users already need to know what they're doing here.

Clear would be less efficient with reference types since it'd zero out all of them, not just the difference. And you can't use AddRange with APIs that take a span without a temporary buffer. That being said, I can't think of a concrete example for now. Will think about it tomorrow.
It's also worth noting that `Capacity` also supports growing or shrinking, it only doesn't support shrinking below `Count`.

> it only doesn't support shrinking below Count

Right, which is the same situation being discussed here.

> Not throwing is less confusing and makes the API more flexible.

More flexible, sure, less confusing, I'm not convinced. That flexibility has a cost: Capacity doesn't let you drop below the Count because it's lossy. If there aren't known use cases for letting SetCount drop, then I'd rather let the caller know they've made a mistake than silently throw away data.

This API is on CollectionsMarshal, so if there are valid use cases for lowering the count, fine, let's do it... I'd like to understand what those are, though.

> Clear would be less efficient with reference types since it'd zero out all of them, not just the difference

I thought you were suggesting clearing out all of them. If you only want some, then RemoveRange from the end. This is why real scenarios need to be shared, to make it concrete what we're actually enabling, and why.

> Right, which is the same situation being discussed here.

Right, the difference being that setting `Capacity` and having it implicitly modify `Count` seems bad. Where-as the user is directly specifying "set the count" here, so allowing shrinkage can make some sense.

> This API is on CollectionsMarshal, so if there are valid use cases for lowering the count, fine, let's do it... I'd like to understand what those are, though.

The general use-case is the same as for growing it. You want to write custom and efficient algorithms that directly modify the List.

I do think basically every scenario comes down to something that can be achieved with `RemoveRange`. I think the question is really whether we need/want to force users to add additional checks/handling to cover removing "excess data" and whether those will end up forcing algorithms to be more expensive.

> The general use-case is the same as for growing it. You want to write custom and efficient algorithms that directly modify the List.

Can you share a specific real example to help me understand?  All the use cases I've seen have been about growing (e.g. I want to get a span for an appending region I manually fill in, I want to increase the size of the list by X so I can manually poke at the expanded range, etc.).  And in cases where you want to use the list as some sort of efficient pooled growable array, I imagine you'd also possibly not want the clearing overhead when reference types are involved.

Again, I'm not saying we shouldn't allow SetCount to shrink, but there are tradeoffs, and so I want to understand what we're actually getting for it.  Or possibly the advantage to SetCount is we make it _never_ clear the shrunken region, but that has its own downsides.

> A simple example would actually involve growing the list.

Thanks.  But in that example, you may incur significant unnecessary clearing if T is or contains reference types.  I'd think if you cared about efficiency, and if SetCount does clearing, you'd want to avoid this.

Right, I'd personally rather `SetCount` was a very simple API that does the minimum amount of work.

In one of my personal projects I have a `ValueList<T>` implementation, which basically mirrors `List<T>` but is a struct, doesn't track a version, and exposes some helper APIs like `SetCountUnsafe` and `AsSpanUnsafe` directly: https://github.com/terrafx/terrafx/blob/main/sources/Core/Collections/ValueList%601.cs#L327

Such a struct is really meant to be an impl detail and not directly exposed and massively simplifies the ability to create custom collection types (avoids cases where you have `class MyCollection { private List<T> _field; }` and therefore have a triple indirection just to access any item). 

It gets used as some of the backing data stores for my GPU memory manager and allows fast and efficient enumeration and modifications, where appropriate.

-- There is also `UnmanagedValueList<T>` which is similar, but backed by native memory and which uses `nuint` for indexing/sizing: https://source.terrafx.dev/#TerraFX/Collections/UnmanagedValueList%25601.cs,7f6272a02876b2cb
Since we have an existing solution for reducing the count with `RemoveRange`, we can start with throwing now and adjust the behavior if needed based on more user feedback.
Wouldn't such change require the API to be rereviewed?

I agree that `SetCount` throwing would be unexpected. `CollectionsMarshal` is home to several lower-level APIs, so the expectation is that the caller understands what they're doing. Why call it `SetCount` if it only works when you are growing the list?

You can always call `Clear` before `SetCount` to "guarantee" success, but that reads strangely in my opinion:
```cs
if (count < list.Count)
    list.Clear(); // essentially SetCount(0)

CollectionsMarshal.SetCount(list, count);
```

> Wouldn't such change require the API to be rereviewed?

Was this behavior discussed at the API review?

> so the expectation is that the caller understands what they're doing

In which case I'm not sure why we're clearing.  If this is about an advanced developer using this unsafe API to do something that requires them to know what they're doing, why are we forcing additional costs upon the operation when we have no idea what the intent is?

> Was this behavior discussed at the API review?

Yes, the reviewers agreed on it behaving like RemoveRange.

I just watched. Alternatives weren't discussed, that was just explaining what the sample code was doing, or how it would behave if this were exposed as the public Count's setter.

Bottom line, I don't see any meaningful scenario for this to be "unsafe" , support shrinking, _and_ spend cycles clearing the shrunken region. But I'll also drop it, because _the_ use case for this method is to increase the count, so, whatever. I think we're making a mistake, but one that probably won't matter.

> In which case I'm not sure why we're clearing. If this is about an advanced developer using this unsafe API to do something that requires them to know what they're doing, why are we forcing additional costs upon the operation when we have no idea what the intent is?

I agree. While I don't expect it to be even remotely close to the "common" use case for the API, I _can_ think of scenarios where not having the clearing behavior for reference types could be potentially beneficial.

For example, using a `List<T>` as a temporary buffer for several operations that may resize it, and then at the end you can `SetCount(Capacity)` followed by `Clear` to ensure objects aren't held onto afterwards, rather than potentially having multiple instances of zeroing inside the actual operation.

But the counterpoint is that this makes the API prone to memory leaks when `T` is a reference type... I'd argue that's grounds to mark the API with `[UnsafeCallersOnly]` if that existed, but at present I think this is a question of "how unsafe is *too* unsafe for `CollectionsMarshal`".

I personally think that if it's appropriately documented, it should be fine to not have the clearing behavior (and as mentioned, it's expected that callers would understand how the API behaves before using it).

> and then at the end you can SetCount(Capacity) followed by Clear to ensure objects aren't held onto afterwards

Sure. But that's just RemoveRange.

> I'd argue that's grounds to mark the API with [UnsafeCallersOnly] if that existed

I expect pretty much everything on `Unsafe`, `Marshal`, `MemoryMarshal`, and `CollectionsMarshal` would be UnsafeCallersOnly if it ever exists.

In the name of making forward progress here, let's finish this PR with the behavior of supporting shrinking and clearing, and then we can have a follow-up conversation about whether to change the behavior prior to shipping.  Along with this, it'd be good to structure the method in a way that optimizes for the expected case of calling this to increase the count.

This API should be optimized for the cases that do not require buffer resizing, with increasing being the main target. Operations that require a resize could potentially be moved into a separate non inlineable local method.
Right.
